stem: A developer needs EC2 capacity for a short, unpredictable test that can't be interrupted, with no long-term commitment.

options.why: On-Demand charges per second or hour with no commitment and no interruptions.
RIs require a one- or three-year commitment.
Dedicated Hosts are for licensing or compliance needs and cost more.
Spot can be interrupted, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

explanation.answer: On-Demand Instances let you pay for compute by the second or hour with no long-term commitments.
explanation.concept: Best for short-term, spiky or unpredictable workloads that can't be interrupted.
explanation.examTip: Short, unpredictable, no interruptions = On-Demand.

stem: A company runs image-rendering jobs that can stop and restart at any time and wants the lowest possible compute price.

options.why: RIs need a commitment and suit steady workloads.
Spot uses spare capacity at up to 90% off On-Demand, suitable for interruptible work.
Dedicated Instances cost more, so it doesn't meet this requirement.
On-Demand is reliable but more expensive.

explanation.answer: Spot Instances use spare EC2 capacity at steep discounts but can be reclaimed by AWS with a two-minute warning.
explanation.concept: Ideal for batch, CI/CD, rendering and other flexible workloads.
explanation.examTip: Interruptible + cheapest = Spot.

stem: A company runs a database server on the same EC2 instance type 24/7 and will for the next three years.
prompt: Which option gives the BIGGEST discount for this steady use?

options.text: On-Demand Instances billed per second with no commitment
options.why: On-Demand has no discount, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

options.text: A one-year commitment with no upfront payment
options.why: One-year, no-upfront terms give smaller discounts.

options.text: A three-year commitment paid all upfront
options.why: Longer terms and more upfront payment give the largest discounts.

options.text: Spot Instances that can be interrupted at short notice
options.why: Spot can interrupt a database server, which isn't what this scenario needs.

explanation.answer: Reserved Instances and Savings Plans give the largest discounts for three-year terms paid all upfront, for steady, predictable usage.
explanation.concept: Discounts can be up to 72% compared with On-Demand.
explanation.examTip: Steady 24/7 for years = 3-year commitment, all upfront for the max discount.

stem: A company wants a discount in exchange for committing to a consistent amount of compute spend per hour, while keeping flexibility to change instance families and Regions.

options.why: Standard RIs are tied to specific instance attributes.
Spot isn't a commitment discount, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.
Dedicated Hosts are physical servers, so it doesn't meet this requirement.
Compute Savings Plans apply to any instance family, size, Region, OS and tenancy, plus Fargate and Lambda.

explanation.answer: Savings Plans offer lower prices for a commitment to a consistent amount of usage (in $/hour) for one or three years.
explanation.concept: Compute Savings Plans are the most flexible; EC2 Instance Savings Plans give more discount but less flexibility.
explanation.examTip: $/hour commitment with flexibility = Compute Savings Plans.

stem: A company's compliance rules require that its EC2 instances run on hardware that isn't shared with other AWS customers. It doesn't need control over instance placement on specific servers.
prompt: Which option fits BEST at the lowest cost?

options.why: Dedicated Instances run on hardware dedicated to one customer.
Dedicated Hosts add server-level control that isn't required here.
These can share hardware with other customers.
Spot runs on shared capacity, which isn't what this scenario needs.

explanation.answer: Dedicated Instances run in a VPC on hardware dedicated to a single customer.
explanation.concept: Dedicated Hosts add visibility and control over the physical server, often for licensing.
explanation.examTip: Single-tenant hardware, no host control needed = Dedicated Instances.

stem: A company must be sure it can launch 50 instances of a specific type in one AZ during a product launch next week, without a long-term commitment.

options.why: Spot capacity isn't guaranteed, which isn't what this scenario needs.
Capacity Reservations reserve capacity in a specific AZ for any duration.
Savings Plans give discounts but don't reserve capacity.
This doesn't guarantee capacity either, which isn't what this scenario needs.

explanation.answer: On-Demand Capacity Reservations reserve compute capacity in a specific AZ for any duration, billed at On-Demand rates whether used or not.
explanation.concept: Combine with Savings Plans for discounts.
explanation.examTip: Guarantee capacity in an AZ, no commitment = On-Demand Capacity Reservation.

stem: A company wants a Reserved Instance discount but expects to change instance families during the term.

options.why: Spot isn't a reservation, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.
These aren't the flexible option and aren't generally available for new purchases.
Convertible RIs can be exchanged for different instance families, OS and tenancy.
Standard RIs can't be exchanged for different instance families.

explanation.answer: Convertible Reserved Instances offer a discount and let you exchange them for RIs with different attributes during the term.
explanation.concept: Standard RIs give a bigger discount but less flexibility.
explanation.examTip: Need to change instance family later = Convertible RI (or Compute Savings Plan).

stem: A company asks how AWS charges for data transfer.

options.text: Transfer in and out of AWS is free in every Region
options.why: Data transfer out to the internet is charged.

options.text: Every transfer costs the same per GB in every Region
options.why: Prices vary by Region and destination, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

options.text: Inbound is charged per GB; outbound to the internet is free
options.why: This is reversed, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: Inbound from the internet is free; outbound is charged
options.why: This is the general AWS data transfer pricing model.

explanation.answer: Data transfer into AWS from the internet is generally free. Data transfer out to the internet and between Regions is charged per GB.
explanation.concept: Data transfer within the same AZ using private IPs is often free; between AZs is charged.
explanation.examTip: In = free. Out = charged.

stem: Before building, a company wants to estimate the monthly cost of a planned architecture on AWS.

options.why: The Pricing Calculator estimates costs for architectures you plan to build.
CUR shows detailed actual usage, so it doesn't meet this requirement.
Budgets track spending against limits, so it doesn't meet this requirement.
Cost Explorer analyzes past and current spending, not planned architectures.

explanation.answer: AWS Pricing Calculator lets you estimate the cost of AWS services for your use case before you build.
explanation.concept: Estimates can be saved and shared.
explanation.examTip: Estimate before building = Pricing Calculator.

stem: A company wants an email alert when its monthly AWS spending is forecast to exceed $5,000.

options.why: The Pricing Calculator estimates planned costs; it doesn't alert.
Budgets set cost or usage thresholds and send alerts, including on forecasts.
Trusted Advisor gives recommendations, not budget alerts.
CloudTrail logs API calls, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

explanation.answer: AWS Budgets lets you set custom cost and usage budgets and alerts you when actual or forecasted amounts exceed them.
explanation.concept: Budget actions can apply IAM or SCP controls automatically.
explanation.examTip: Alert when spend will exceed X = AWS Budgets.

references.title: Managing your costs with AWS Budgets

stem: A finance manager wants to visualize spending over the last 12 months by service and see a forecast.

options.why: Artifact provides compliance reports, so it doesn't meet this requirement.
The Pricing Calculator estimates planned architectures.
Cost Explorer visualizes historical costs and forecasts future spending.
Inspector scans for vulnerabilities, which isn't what this scenario needs.

explanation.answer: AWS Cost Explorer lets you view and analyze costs and usage with graphs, filters and forecasts.
explanation.concept: It also provides RI and Savings Plans recommendations.
explanation.examTip: Analyze past spend + forecast = Cost Explorer.

stem: A company wants the most detailed, line-item billing data delivered to Amazon S3 for its own analysis.

options.text: AWS Budgets reports emailed on a schedule
options.why: These summarize budget status, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: AWS Pricing Calculator estimates exported to CSV
options.why: This estimates planned costs, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

options.text: AWS Cost Explorer graphs grouped by service
options.why: Cost Explorer visualizes and filters costs, but the Cost and Usage Report is the most detailed line-item data delivered to S3.

options.text: AWS Cost and Usage Reports (via Data Exports)
options.why: CUR delivers detailed line-item cost and usage data to S3.

explanation.answer: The AWS Cost and Usage Report provides the most comprehensive cost and usage data, delivered to an S3 bucket for analysis.
explanation.concept: Data Exports can deliver CUR 2.0 and query it with Athena or QuickSight.
explanation.examTip: Most detailed billing data = Cost and Usage Report.

stem: A company has 12 AWS accounts and wants one bill and combined usage for volume discounts.

options.why: Consolidated billing gives one bill and aggregates usage across accounts.

options.text: Separate credit cards for each account
options.why: This keeps bills separate, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.
Cost Explorer analyzes costs but doesn't combine billing.
Budgets track spending; they don't combine bills.

explanation.answer: Consolidated billing combines usage across accounts in an organization, producing one bill and possibly lower tiered prices.
explanation.concept: Reserved Instance and Savings Plans discounts can be shared across accounts.
explanation.examTip: One bill + shared volume discounts = consolidated billing.

stem: A company wants to see costs broken down by project and department in its bills.

options.why: Security groups don't appear as cost categories.
Activated tags let you group costs by project or department.
These set password rules, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: Separate AWS Regions for each department
options.why: Regions aren't a cost attribution tool, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

explanation.answer: Cost allocation tags label resources so you can organize and track costs by categories such as project, team or environment.
explanation.concept: Tags must be activated in the Billing console to appear in cost reports.
explanation.examTip: Costs by project/team = cost allocation tags.

stem: A student wants to understand what the AWS Free Tier offers.

options.text: Every AWS service is free for the first year at any usage level
options.why: The Free Tier has usage limits; it doesn't make every service free at any level.

options.text: Access requires a paid Enterprise Support plan to activate
options.why: The Free Tier is available to new and eligible customers without a paid support plan.

options.text: Free usage of many services, within set limits and time periods
options.why: The Free Tier offers free usage up to specified limits, with some offers time-limited.

options.text: Unlimited EC2 usage of any instance type for one year
options.why: Free Tier compute is limited, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

explanation.answer: The AWS Free Tier lets eligible customers try many services free within limits. Some offers are always free; others are time-limited or credit-based.
explanation.concept: Usage beyond limits is billed at normal rates.
explanation.examTip: Free Tier = free within limits; watch usage.

stem: A company asks what drives its Amazon S3 bill.

options.text: Mainly the length of the bucket names that are chosen
options.why: This doesn't affect price, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: Mainly the number of buckets created in the account
options.why: Bucket count isn't a main cost driver, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

options.text: Mainly the number of IAM users that access the buckets
options.why: IAM users aren't billed, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

options.text: Storage amount and class, requests, retrieval and data out
options.why: These are the main S3 cost factors, so it meets the requirement described here.

explanation.answer: S3 pricing depends on storage used and storage class, requests and data retrievals, data transfer out and optional features.
explanation.concept: Choosing the right storage class can greatly reduce costs.
explanation.examTip: S3 cost = GB stored (by class) + requests + retrieval + transfer out.

stem: A company asks how AWS Lambda is billed.

options.text: Per number of requests and compute duration
options.why: Lambda charges for requests and duration, based on memory allocated.

options.text: Per server hour, whether used or not
options.why: Lambda doesn't bill for idle servers, so it doesn't meet this requirement.
Code size doesn't drive pricing, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: A fixed monthly fee per function
options.why: Lambda has no fixed fee per function, which isn't what this scenario needs.

explanation.answer: Lambda charges for the number of requests and the duration your code runs, measured in GB-seconds based on memory.
explanation.concept: A free tier includes a set number of requests and compute time each month.
explanation.examTip: Lambda = requests + duration × memory.

stem: A company wants to be alerted automatically when spending on a service suddenly jumps in an unusual way.

options.why: This estimates planned costs, so it doesn't meet this requirement.
Cost Anomaly Detection uses ML to find unusual spending and alert you.
Polly converts text to speech, so it doesn't meet this requirement.
Artifact provides compliance reports, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

explanation.answer: AWS Cost Anomaly Detection uses machine learning to monitor costs and alert you to unusual spending.
explanation.concept: It complements fixed-threshold alerts from AWS Budgets.
explanation.examTip: Unusual spend spikes = Cost Anomaly Detection.

references.title: Detecting unusual spend with AWS Cost Anomaly Detection

stem: A company is matching pricing models to workloads.
prompt: Which TWO pairings are MOST cost-effective? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Steady 24/7 web servers for three years – Savings Plans
options.why: Commitment discounts fit steady usage, so it meets the requirement described here.

options.text: A short unpredictable test – Dedicated Hosts
options.why: Dedicated Hosts add cost without benefit here.
Interruptions would disrupt a steady database.

options.text: A two-day test – three-year Reserved Instances
options.why: A long commitment for a short test wastes money.
Spot gives deep discounts for interruptible work.

explanation.answer: Match pricing to workload: Spot for interruptible, Savings Plans/RIs for steady, On-Demand for short or unpredictable.
explanation.concept: Many architectures combine all three.
explanation.examTip: Steady=commit, flexible=Spot, short/unknown=On-Demand.

stem: A manager asks what AWS's general pricing principles are.
prompt: Which TWO statements describe AWS pricing? (Select TWO.)

options.why: You pay for services as you use them, so it meets the requirement described here.

options.text: Pay less when you reserve or commit
options.why: Commitments like Savings Plans lower prices.

options.text: Pay extra for using the Management Console
options.why: The console is free, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

options.text: Pay the same regardless of how much you use
options.why: Prices often decrease per unit with volume.

options.text: Pay a mandatory setup fee for every service
options.why: Most services have no setup fee, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

explanation.answer: AWS pricing principles: pay as you go, save when you commit, and pay less per unit by using more (volume tiers).
explanation.concept: AWS also has lowered prices many times as its scale grew.
explanation.examTip: Pay as you go, save when you commit, pay less by using more.
